fact_en:
Why can't we see water vapor?

Water vapor is an invisible gas! Clouds only appear when it cools and condenses into visible liquid water droplets.
fact_bis:
Ngano nga dili makita ang water vapor?

Ang water vapor kay dili makita nga gas! Mogawas lang ang panganod kung mokunhod kini ug mag-condense ngadto sa makita nga liquid water droplets.

findings.note: The cooling step of cloud formation is replaced by a quantity change. EN: "Clouds only appear when it cools and condenses into visible liquid water droplets." BIS: "Mogawas lang ang panganod kung mokunhod kini ug mag-condense..." — 'mokunhod' is to DECREASE/lessen, used that way in 218 cards of this corpus; cooling is mobugnaw, which the sibling card ffct-34800 in this same batch uses correctly ("mosaka, mobugnaw, ug mahimong gagmayng tulo sa tubig"). A Cebuano-only child learns clouds appear when water vapour DIMINISHES rather than when it cools. Lower confidence / lower severity: the card's actual question ("why can't we see water vapor?") is still answered correctly, and 'mag-condense' survives.

fact_en:
Why is Baguio City often covered in thick fog?

Warm, moist air travels up high! When it cools and condenses at high elevations, it creates the thick fog Baguio City is famous for.
fact_bis:
Nganong kasagaran nga makasinati og daghang panganod ang Baguio City?

Moakyat ang init ug mamasa nga hangin! Kung mo-cool down ug mo-condense sa taas nga lugar, makahimo kini og makabag-on nga panganod sa Baguio City.

findings.note: title_bis "Yabo sa Baguio" for "Fog in Baguio" — yabo is to spill/pour out a liquid; Cebuano fog is gabon (gabun). The body never uses a fog word either (it renders "thick fog" as "makabag-on nga panganod" = cloud), so nothing in the card restores it. Systemic: the same yabo=fog swap recurs in other batches ("Yabo nga Panganod sa Yuta", "Yabo sa Dalan").

fact_en:
How does thick fog form in high places like Baguio?

Cooling water vapor condenses into tiny liquid droplets! This is how thick fog forms in the chilly air.
fact_bis:
Unsaon paghimo sa daghang fog sa mga taas nga dapit sama sa Baguio?

Ang nagbugnaw nga water vapor mo-condense ngadto sa gagmay nga patak sa likido nga tubig! Mao ni ang paghimo sa daghang fog.

findings.note: Same defective title as ffct-34846: "Yabo sa Baguio" = "Spill in Baguio" for "Fog in Baguio" (correct: gabon). Here the body keeps the English "fog", so the Cebuano card offers no correct Cebuano word for fog and the title asserts a different thing.

fact_en: Terraced rice fields like in Banaue are flat steps carved into a mountainside. They stop soil from washing away and hold water for crops!
fact_bis: Ang hagdan-hagdan nga palayan sama sa Banaue mga patag nga steps nga gikulit sa mountainside. Pugngan niini ang pag-agnas sa yuta ug tipigan ang tubig alang sa tanom!

findings.note: title_bis "Pagsaka sa Terrace" for "Terrace Farming" — Tagalog false friend: Tagalog pagsasaka = farming, but Cebuano saka = to CLIMB/go up, so the title reads "Climbing the Terrace". Cebuano farming is pag-uma / pagpanguma. The body is about erosion control and water retention in hagdan-hagdan nga palayan and never says uma, so the title's claim (climbing) is not corrected.

fact_en: The Apollo 11 astronauts landed on the Moon's Sea of Tranquility, marking the very first human visit to another celestial body!
fact_bis: Ang mga astronaut sa Apollo 11 milukso sa Sea of Tranquility sa Moon, nga mao ang unang pagbisita sa tawo sa laing celestial body!

findings.note: Lower confidence than the others, but the landing verb is wrong in BOTH fields with no restoration: title "Lupad sa Tranquility" (lupad = flight/to fly) for "Landing at Tranquility", and body "milukso sa Sea of Tranquility" (milukso = jumped/leapt) for "landed on" (nitugpa / milanding). A Cebuano-only reader gets astronauts jumping/flying, never landing; only "unang pagbisita sa tawo" hints at arrival.

fact_en:
How do basalt rocks form?

Dark, fine-grained basalt rocks form when hot lava from Philippine volcanoes cools rapidly on the surface.
fact_bis:
Unsaon paghimo sa basalt rocks?

Ang ngitngit, pinong basalt rocks nagmugna kung ang init nga lava gikan sa mga bulkan sa Pilipinas dali ra nga nagkaluoy sa ibabaw.

findings.note: Body: "ang init nga lava ... dali ra nga nagkaluoy sa ibabaw" — nagkaluoy = became pitiful / took pity, not cooled (mibugnaw / dali nga nabugnaw). The whole fact of the card is that basalt is fine-grained BECAUSE the lava cools rapidly at the surface; with nagkaluoy the cooling step is gone and nothing else in the card restores it, so a Cebuano-only reader cannot answer "how does basalt form?". The title compounds it: "Pagbukad sa Basalt" (bukad = to bloom/open out) for "How Basalt Forms" (pagkaporma / unsaon pagkabuo).

fact_en: Dark forest topsoil contains humus! It is made of fully decomposed leaves and dead organisms that enrich the earth.
fact_bis: Ang ngitngit nga topsoil sa lasang adunay humus! Himo kini sa hingpit nga nabungkag nga mga dahon ug patay nga organismo nga nagpasig-uli sa yuta.

findings.note: title_bis "Humus sa Kagahuman" for title_en "Forest Humus". Kagahuman is from gahum = power/authority (dominion), not forest; Cebuano forest is lasang/kagubatan/kalasangan. The card's OWN body uses the correct word ("topsoil sa LASANG"), which is the title-outlier signal. Read alone, the title names a different thing entirely.

fact_en:
Why don't planets fly away into deep space?

The Sun's massive gravity constantly pulls planets toward it, keeping them in curved elliptical orbits instead of flying into deep space!
fact_bis:
Nganong dili molupad ang mga planeta palayo sa lawom nga kalawakan?

Ang kusog kaayo nga grabidad sa Adlaw kanunay nga nagdani sa mga planeta, mao nga magpabilin sila sa kurbado nga elliptical nga orbit imbes nga molupad palayo!

findings.note: title_bis "Ngano Dili Mupakpak" for title_en "Why Planets Stay Put". In Cebuano pakpak = to clap/applaud (wing is pako; to fly is lupad), so the title reads "Why doesn't it clap" — and the subject (planets) is dropped as well, so the title names nothing recoverable. The card's OWN body uses the correct verb ("Nganong dili MOLUPAD ang mga planeta palayo..."), confirming the title is the outlier rather than dialect variation.

fact_en: The Great Wall of China cannot be seen from space with the naked eye, but astronauts in low orbit can see highways, dams, and cities!
fact_bis: Dili makita sa mata ang Great Wall of China gikan sa kalibutan, apan makit-an sa mga astronaut nga naa sa low orbit ang mga highway, dam, ug siyudad!

findings.note: Body: EN "cannot be seen from space with the naked eye" becomes "Dili makita sa mata ang Great Wall of China gikan sa KALIBUTAN" — kalibutan is world/Earth in Cebuano (space is kalawakan/kawanangan, which card ffct-35069 itself uses). The Cebuano therefore asserts the Wall cannot be seen from Earth, which is plainly false and is the exact opposite framing of the myth the card exists to bust. The second clause ("astronauts in low orbit can see highways, dams, cities") is about highways, not the Wall, so nothing in the card restores "from space". A child reading only the Cebuano ends up believing something false.

fact_en: If caught outside during a thunderstorm, crouch low with your feet together to minimize ground contact and avoid lightning strikes!
fact_bis: Kung naa ka gawas samtang nag-bagyo, lingkodi ang lawas ug ipundok ang mga tiil aron dili ka dali ma-igo sa kidlat!

findings.note: Lightning-safety action is changed and its reason dropped. EN: "crouch low with your feet together to minimize ground contact". BIS: "lingkodi ang lawas ug ipundok ang mga tiil" — lingkod = TO SIT (the listed false friend), so the card tells a child to SIT DOWN in a thunderstorm, which increases ground contact instead of minimising it; the 'minimize ground contact' clause is also gone. The corpus's own lightning card ffct-24485 uses the correct word for the same instruction: "Daliana og pungko". Title 'Yukbo sa Kilat' is fine; the body is the outlier.

fact_en:
Why is it dangerous to look at a solar eclipse without special glasses?

Looking directly at one without special glasses can permanently damage your retinas and cause blindness!
fact_bis:
Nganong delikado mutan-aw sa solar eclipse nga walay espesyal nga glasses?

Ang diretso nga pagtan-aw nga walay espesyal nga glasses mahimong ma-daot ang retina nimo ug mag-resulta sa pagkabulag!

findings.note: Eclipse-safety outcome becomes a different thing. EN: "can permanently damage your retinas and cause blindness". BIS: "mag-resulta sa pagkabulag" — in Cebuano bulag = TO SEPARATE (this corpus uses it exactly that way for chromatography, ffct-17574 'magkabulag sila', and for splitting light, ffct-35097 'mo-bulag sa pito ka kolor'). Blind in Cebuano is buta/pagkabuta. The card's stated consequence reads as 'results in separation'; the word blindness is never restored on the card.

fact_en:
How much of Earth's water is salty?

Approximately 97 percent of all water on Earth is salty! You can find this salty water in our five major oceans.
fact_bis:
Pila ka porsyento sa tubig sa Kalibutan ang asin?

Mga 97 porsyento sa tanang tubig sa Kalibutan kay asin! Makita nimo ang asin nga tubig sa lima ka dagkong kadagatan.

findings.note: title_bis is corrupted text, not Cebuano: "97% Tubig ASA Asoy" for "97% of Water Is Salty" — asa = where, asoy = to narrate/recount; neither means salty, and the stray all-caps ASA looks like a mangled token. The body is correct and uses asin ('Mga 97 porsyento sa tanang tubig sa Kalibutan kay asin'), so a reader recovers the fact from the body, but the shipped title itself is unreadable rather than merely terse — unlike the acceptable compact-title style, it names nothing. Lowest-severity flag here; included because the defect is in the title and is not register or regional variation.
